Document Title: Two Shots are Enough: Reliable Constrained Generation with LLMs
Authors: M. Mondal; L. Dolamic; P. Cudré-Mauroux; J. Audiffren
Author Affiliations: University of Fribourg, Fribourg, Switzerland; armasuisse W+T, Thun, Switzerland; University of Fribourg, Fribourg, Switzerland; University of Fribourg, Fribourg, Switzerland
Publication Title: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Big Data (BigData)
Abstract: Despite exhibiting impressive performance across many complex tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle to consistently produce structured responses, a key element in many applications such as agent orchestration. While template-based methods or in-context learning can improve structure compliance, constrained decoding and additional context have been shown to skew the distribution of the responses and may result in suboptimal performance. In this work, we show that the number of in-context examples is a key factor: in many settings, one to two shots are sufficient to reliably produce the predefined structures, while additional examples may degrade the response quality. Our analysis shows that this phenomenon is consistent across a wide range of datasets, models, and structures and indicates that providing this small number of shots achieves the best overall trade-off between structure compliance and response correctness while improving the results of constrained generation methods such as template-based approaches.
Author Keywords: Large Language Models;In-context Learning;Constrained Generation;Structured Output

Authors: K. Zhang; W. Yu; J. Xu
Author Affiliations: Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence, Renmin University of China; School of Information Technology and Management, University of International Business and Economics; Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence, Renmin University of China
Publication Title: ICASSP 2026 - 2026 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP)
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to legal tasks to assist judges and lawyers in decision-making, where outputs must remain faithful to case facts and legal elements to ensure reliable legal interpretations and accurate predictions. Existing approaches—ranging from prompt engineering to task-specific fine-tuning—either demand substantial human effort or lack explicit mechanisms to guarantee such fidelity. To address this issue, we propose Fidelity-Constrained Decoding (FCD), a tuning-free decoding framework that directly constrains generation to preserve strict alignment with both factual details and legal elements. Experiments on three legal datasets with two open-domain LLMs show that FCD consistently improves performance across diverse legal reasoning tasks while avoiding additional training overhead. Our code and datasets are available at https://github.com/ke-01/FCD.

Abstract: Controlling the behavior of large language models (LLMs) at inference time is essential for aligning outputs with human abilities and safety requirements. Activation steering provides a lightweight alternative to prompt engineering and fine-tuning by directly modifying internal activations to guide generation. This research advances the literature in three significant directions. First, while previous work demonstrated the technical feasibility of steering emotional tone using automated classifiers, this paper presents the first human evaluation of activation steering concerning the emotional tone of LLM outputs, collecting over 7,000 crowd-sourced ratings from 190 participants via Prolific ( $n=190$ ). These ratings assess both perceived emotional intensity and overall text quality. Second, we find strong alignment between human and model-based quality ratings (mean  $r=0.776$ , range 0.157–0.985), indicating automatic scoring can proxy perceived quality. Moderate steering strengths ( $\lambda \approx 0.15$ ) reliably amplify target emotions while preserving comprehensibility, with the strongest effects for disgust ( $\eta _{p}^{2} = 0.616$ ) and fear ( $\eta _{p}^{2} = 0.540$ ), and minimal effects for surprise ( $\eta _{p}^{2} = 0.042$ ). Finally, upgrading from Alpaca to LlaMA-3 yielded more consistent steering with significant effects across emotions and strengths (all  $p \lt 0.001$ ). Inter-rater reliability was high (ICC = 0.71–0.87), underscoring the robustness of the findings. These findings support activation-based control as a scalable method for steering LLM behavior across affective dimensions.

Authors: Y. Wang; Q. Huang; K. Wu; K. Guo
Author Affiliations: School of Information Engineering, Zhongnan University of Economics and Law, Wuhan, China; School of Information Engineering, Zhongnan University of Economics and Law, Wuhan, China; Beijing Peony Electronic Group Co., Ltd., Beijing, China; School of Information Engineering, Zhongnan University of Economics and Law, Wuhan, China
Publication Title: 2025 IEEE 24th International Conference on Trust, Security and Privacy in Computing and Communications (TrustCom)
Abstract: The detection of offensive language in social media faces significant challenges due to its diverse and evolving expressions, making accurate identification remains critical for maintaining healthy online ecosystems. While few-shot learning with large language models (LLMs) has demonstrated potential in this domain, conventional static demonstration selection strategies often fail to adapt to the linguistic variability of offensive content, which ultimately limits model performance. To address this limitation, we propose LLMs with Dynamic Few-Shot (LDFS), a novel method that encodes the training set into dense vector representations, retrieves top-k nearest-neighbors for each sample, and constructs balanced demonstrations by strategically sampling from offensive and non-offensive classes. These demonstrations are integrated with the task description and output constraints to construct structured prompts that guide the LLMs to perform the classification. Comprehensive evaluations on the benchmark datasets COLDataset and CDial-Bias reveal that LDFS consistently outperforms conventional approaches. The method achieves superior performance compared to random 10-shot selection, with F1-score improvements reaching up to 14 percentage points. Notably, LDFS surpasses specialized fine-tuned models including COLDETECTOR by 6.82% and GLM2 P-Prompt by 17.47% in F1-score on the CDial-Bias dataset. These results demonstrate that dynamic, semantically-aware demonstration selection can effectively enhance the capability of LLMs to recognize offensive language across diverse contexts.

Abstract: Traditionally, constructing a professional simulation deduction script is a long-cycle process that requires collaboration between domain experts and simulation experts. The increasing demands for simulation deduction across large-scale scenarios and emergency situations highlight the need for rapid simulation scenario construction methods. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer powerful new tools to address these challenges. In this work, we propose LLM-HABG, a highly portable framework that can automatically generate behavior plans for heterogeneous agents in urban simulation environments based on natural language instructions, requiring no additional post-training. It comprises four stages: task extraction, task decomposition and allocation, urban information retrieval, and behavior generation. To overcome the limitations of LLMs, such as deficient instruction-following and hallucinations, we incorporate a suite of enhancement techniques including dynamic few-shot learning, entity alignment, and constrained decoding. Experimental results demonstrate that LLM-HABG achieves robust performance even with 14B-parameter models, attaining a success rate exceeding 75 %-nearly doubling baseline performance. This conversational behavior configuration paradigm empowers domain experts to interact directly with simulation systems via natural language, significantly reducing the cost and barriers associated with simulation scenario construction.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming biomedical text mining, yet their reliability in extracting precise drug-effect relations remains uncertain. In this work, we take three state-of-the-art open-source models—Mistral, Qwen, and Gemma-beyond generic benchmarks and place them under a stress test that exposes the fine line between accuracy, structural discipline, and hallucination. We evaluate their ability to extract structured (drug, effect) pairs from real biomedical narratives, measuring task-specific F1 scores, semantic hallucination penalties, JSON compliance, and inference speed. The results reveal striking contrasts: Qwen excels in structured fidelity, Mistral achieves strong accuracy but at the cost of higher hallucination rates, and Gemma delivers stable outputs only under low-complexity scenarios. Ten indepth visual analyses uncover hidden trade-offs that influence deployment choices in high-stakes medical NLP. The study offers concrete strategies-prompt engineering, constrained decoding, and fine-tuning-to bridge the gap between LLM potential and clinical-grade reliability.

Publication Title: IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech and Language Processing
Abstract: Error correction (EC) models play a crucial role in refining Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) transcriptions, enhancing the readability and quality of transcriptions. Without requiring access to the underlying code or model weights, EC can improve performance and provide domain adaptation for black-box ASR systems. This work investigates the use of large language models (LLMs) for error correction across diverse scenarios. 1-best ASR hypotheses are commonly used as the input to EC models. We propose building high-performance EC models using ASR N-best lists which should provide more contextual information for the correction process. Additionally, the generation process of a standard EC model is unrestricted in the sense that any output sequence can be generated. For some scenarios, such as unseen domains, this flexibility may impact performance. To address this, we introduce a constrained decoding approach based on the N-best list or an ASR lattice. Finally, most EC models are trained for a specific ASR system requiring retraining whenever the underlying ASR system is changed. This paper explores the ability of EC models to operate on the output of different ASR systems. This concept is further extended to zero-shot error correction using LLMs, such as ChatGPT. Experiments on three standard datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed methods for both Transducer and attention-based encoder-decoder ASR systems. In addition, the proposed method can serve as an effective method for model ensembling.

Publication Title: 2026 IEEE 6th International Conference on Smart Information Systems and Technologies (SIST)
Abstract: Providing quality healthcare is a key goal of governments worldwide. There are enormous challenges, including the high cost of medical care, timeliness of treatments, and the optimization of available resources. The use of AI is emerging as a key technology to address some of these challenges. We focus on the use of clinical calculators, which are a key component in decision-support systems. We aim to automatically compute patient vitals from unstructured clinical notes to enhance workflow efficiency. However, this task remains an open challenge for language models. We investigate two complementary strategies for medical score calculation using the Qwen3-4B-Instruct small language model on eight rule-based calculators from the MedCalc-Bench benchmark: CHA2DS2-VASc, Centor, HEART, PERC, and SIRS. First, we develop a two-stage structured prompt that decomposes each task into entity extraction followed by rule application. Second, we apply supervised fine-tuning with QLoRA (4-bit NormalFloat quantization and low-rank adapters), attaining 60.0% accuracy on the same evaluation set. Comparative analysis reveals that structured prompting outperforms QLoRA fine-tuning on this subset, while fine-tuning yields superior format adherence and reduced hallucination. We also found that roughly half the SIRS test cases in MedCalc-Bench have incorrect labels, artificially limiting how well any model can perform. We determined that our model performance is insensitive to LoRA rank and learning rate within tested ranges. These findings offer practical guidance for deploying small language models in resource-constrained clinical AI settings.

Publication Title: 2026 International Conference on Generative Artificial Intelligence and Information Security (GAIIS)
Abstract: Abstractive text summarization is a core challenge in natural language processing (NLP), and deploying large language models (LLMs) in this setting exposes three critical limitations: (1) LLMs tend to ignore semantically central content due to unstructured input representations, leading to uninformative summaries; (2) standard fine-tuning objectives fail to align NLP generation pipelines with human preferences for factual fidelity, resulting in entity-level and relational hallucinations; and (3) existing decoding strategies impose no length or faithfulness constraints, producing verbose or factually inconsistent outputs. To address these shortcomings, we propose FLAP (Faithful LLM-Aligned Prompting), a two-stage NLP framework that integrates (1) a saliency-guided Semantic Prompt Encoder that selects and re-weights semantically central sentences via a primacy–recency positional bias, (2) a composite reward model combining lexical, semantic faithfulness, and conciseness signals to drive Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for human-aligned NLP generation, and (3) a constrained decoding strategy that jointly enforces target length and entailment-based faithfulness at inference time. Extensive experiments on CNN/DailyMail, XSum, and Reddit across LLM backbone scales from 7B to 70B demonstrate that FLAP consistently outperforms strong NLP baselines in ROUGE, BERTScore, BARTScore, and human evaluation, while reducing hallucination rates by up to 25.1 percentage points.

Abstract: Despite the renewed interest in zero-shot visual classification due to the rise of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), the problem of evaluating free-form responses of auto-regressive models remains a persistent challenge. Most existing works focus on language-only tasks or don’t consider Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs) beyond 5-way options, both of which are critical capabilities to solve tasks in Fine-Grained Visual Classification (FGVC) where choice counts are in the hundreds to thousands and the choices are highly related. Furthermore, in this highly multi-way MCQ setting it is not clear how to extend LLM choice extraction to retrieval-based problems, where computing probabilities over the choice set is computationally costly. In this work we investigate nlg2choice, a simple two-stage method which first asks the MLLM an open-ended question for the task with minimal constraints, then uses text-only constrained decoding to predict the most likely choice. In retrieval settings, we compute the probability of the constrained response taking that choice with an early stopping method to significantly improve throughput. Our results show improvement over a suite of seven fine-grained visual datasets when evaluating in terms of classification and retrieval, and show that this performance holds over the various ways that users of LLMs can implement tasks in natural language.

Document Title: Large Language Model Assistant for Updating and Managing Asset Administration Shells
Authors: D. Becker; C. Rosenhauer; G. Frey
Abstract: Natural-language access to Asset Administration Shell (AAS) repositories could lower the barrier for interaction with standardized digital twins, especially for users who are unfamiliar with AAS structures and APIs. While prior work has explored AI support for the AAS lifecycle through the generation or semantic mapping of AAS content, empirical studies on local large language models (LLMs) for direct interaction with deployed AAS repositories remain limited, especially in systematically evaluated staged settings. This paper presents a multi-stage assistant for natural-language-based management of AAS data hosted in Eclipse BaSyx. The approach decomposes the task into multi-staged processing steps for shell identification, deeper submodel or element-level operation generation, and user-facing response formulation. To improve robustness of machine-readable intermediate outputs, the system employs grammar-constrained decoding and prompt-based conditioning with zero-shot and few-shot configurations. The evaluation compares three quantized models in the 8 billion parameter range: Llama 3.1, DeepSeek R1, and Qwen 3, on a task set covering retrieval, modification, and general interaction scenarios across multiple query formulations. The results show that few-shot prompting is essential for reliable performance, whereas zero-shot prompting is insufficient for many structured interaction tasks. The best configuration, based on Llama 3.1 8B, achieves an effective success rate of up to 81%, while short and ambiguous queries remain challenging. These findings indicate that small local LLMs can provide a feasible privacy-preserving interface for structured AAS repository interaction when combined with multi-stage task decomposition and constrained decoding.

Abstract: The accelerated digital transformation of banking has fundamentally altered how customers engage with financial institutions, placing unprecedented pressure on customer service systems to deliver fast, accurate, and contextually grounded responses.
